nodes.label: Sacred Groves
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Tracts of forest set aside for worship. Protected by communities for centuries. Found in Rajasthan (Orans), Meghalaya (sacred groves in Khasi and Jaintia hills), Western Ghats (Devvans). Important for conservation.

nodes.label: Forest Types by Legal Status
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Reserved Forests: most restricted, 53% of India's forest area, mainly in dense forests. Protected Forests: some restrictions, 30%. Unclassed Forests: no restrictions, 17%. States like MP, Jharkhand, UP have large reserved forest areas.

nodes.label: India's Water Resources
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India receives nearly 4% of global precipitation. 1869 billion cubic metres of surface water, only 690 bcm utilisable. Growing demand from population, industrialisation, agriculture. Water scarcity increasing despite abundance.

nodes.label: Multipurpose River Valley Projects
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Dams built for irrigation, power generation, flood control, water supply, navigation, fisheries. Called 'temples of modern India' by Nehru. Examples: Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud, Damodar Valley, Nagarjuna Sagar, Sardar Sarovar.

nodes.label: Chota Nagpur Industrial Belt
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India's mineral heartland across Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, WB. Rich in iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica. Concentration of mineral-based industries: TISCO, Bokaro Steel.

nodes.label: Sugar Industry
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India second largest producer. 60% mills in UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka. Seasonal industry. UP dominates in number of mills but Maharashtra has higher per hectare yield. Shifting from north to south.

nodes.label: Iron and Steel Industry (India)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Basic industry providing raw materials to other industries. Major centres: Bhilai, Durgapur, Burnpur, Jamshedpur, Rourkela, Bokaro (Chota Nagpur belt), Bhadravati, Salem, Visakhapatnam. India 4th largest producer.

nodes.label: Transport in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Includes roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways, airways. Essential for economic development. India has one of largest road networks (62 lakh km) and railway networks (68000 km, 4th largest) in the world.

nodes.label: Indian Roads
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 6 types: National Highways (central govt), State Highways (state govts), District Roads, Other Roads (villages), Border Roads (BRO in border areas), Express Highways. Golden Quadrilateral: Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata. NH account for 2% of road length but carry 40% of traffic.

nodes.label: Indian Airways
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Air India (international) and Indian Airlines (now Air India) for domestic. Private airlines: IndiGo, SpiceJet, Vistara. DGCA regulates aviation. Pawan Hans for helicopter services to NE and offshore.

nodes.label: Communication in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Personal: letters, telegraph, telephone, email. Mass: newspapers, radio, TV, cinema, internet. India has 1 billion+ mobile subscribers. BSNL, private telecom. Digital India initiative for connectivity.

nodes.label: Golden Quadrilateral and NSEW Corridor
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: GQ: 5846 km connecting Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata. NSEW Corridor: Srinagar-Kanyakumari and Silchar-Porbandar. NH Development Project for 6-lane expressways. Reduces travel time significantly.

nodes.label: Earth's Crust
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Outermost solid layer of the earth. Continental crust (sial) averages 30-35 km thick (up to 70 km under mountains), oceanic crust (sima) is 5-7 km thick. Continental crust is mainly granitic (silica-alumina), oceanic crust is basaltic (silica-magnesia). Separated from mantle by Mohorovicic discontinuity.

nodes.label: Mantle
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Layer between crust and core extending from Moho (35 km) to 2,900 km depth. Composed of silicate rocks rich in iron and magnesium. Upper mantle includes the asthenosphere (partially molten, convection currents drive plate tectonics). Lower mantle is solid due to high pressure. Contains 84% of earth's volume.

nodes.label: Earth's Core
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Innermost layer from 2,900 km to 6,371 km depth. Outer core is liquid iron-nickel (2,900-5,150 km), generates earth's magnetic field through dynamo effect. Inner core is solid iron-nickel despite extreme temperatures (5,000-6,000C) due to immense pressure. Separated from mantle by Gutenberg discontinuity.

nodes.label: Mohorovicic Discontinuity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Boundary between the crust and mantle discovered by Andrija Mohorovicic in 1909. Located at about 35 km depth under continents and 5-8 km under oceans. Seismic wave velocities increase sharply at this boundary, indicating a change in rock composition and density.

nodes.label: Gutenberg Discontinuity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Boundary between the mantle and outer core at about 2,900 km depth. Named after Beno Gutenberg. P-wave velocity drops sharply and S-waves disappear at this boundary, indicating transition from solid mantle to liquid outer core. Marks the most significant compositional change inside earth.

nodes.label: Sial (Continental Crust)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Upper layer of the earth's crust dominated by silica and alumina, hence the name sial. Forms the continental crust with average density of 2.7 g/cm3. Made primarily of granitic rocks. Thicker under mountain ranges and absent under deep ocean floors.

nodes.label: Sima (Oceanic Crust)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Lower layer of the crust and oceanic crust dominated by silica and magnesia. Denser than sial at 3.0 g/cm3. Made primarily of basaltic rocks. Forms the ocean floor and underlies the sial layer in continental areas. Continuous layer beneath both continents and oceans.

nodes.label: Continental Drift Theory
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Theory proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912 that all continents were once joined as a single landmass (Pangaea) surrounded by a single ocean (Panthalassa). Continents drifted apart over millions of years. Evidence includes jigsaw fit of coastlines, fossil distribution, rock matching, and glacial tillite deposits.

nodes.label: Pangaea
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Supercontinent that existed about 250 million years ago comprising all present-day continents. Name means 'all earth'. Began breaking apart during the Triassic period. First split into Laurasia (northern) and Gondwana (southern) separated by Tethys Sea. Wegener's central concept in continental drift theory.

nodes.label: Laurasia
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Northern supercontinent formed when Pangaea split. Comprised present-day North America, Europe, and Asia. Separated from Gondwana by the Tethys Sea. Further broke apart to form the modern northern continents and the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans.

nodes.label: Gondwana
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Southern supercontinent comprising South America, Africa, India, Australia, and Antarctica. Named after the Gondwana region of India where matching Glossopteris fossils were found. Gondwana system of sediments from India has counterparts in six Southern Hemisphere landmasses. Broke apart in stages during Mesozoic era.

nodes.label: Plate Tectonics Theory
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Modern theory explaining movement of lithospheric plates on the asthenosphere. Earth's lithosphere is divided into major and minor plates. Plate movements driven by convection currents in the mantle. Explains earthquakes, volcanism, mountain building, and ocean floor spreading. Refined version of continental drift.

nodes.label: Convergent Boundary
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Plate boundary where two plates move toward each other. Three types: oceanic-oceanic (forms island arcs like Japan), oceanic-continental (subduction creates trenches and volcanic mountains like Andes), continental-continental (collision creates fold mountains like Himalayas). Also called destructive boundary as lithosphere is consumed.

nodes.label: Divergent Boundary
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Plate boundary where two plates move apart from each other. New crust is formed as magma rises from the asthenosphere. Creates mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys. Example: Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift Valley. Also called constructive boundary as new lithosphere is created.

nodes.label: Transform Boundary
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Plate boundary where two plates slide past each other horizontally. Neither crust is created nor destroyed. Causes earthquakes but no volcanism. Example: San Andreas Fault in California. Also called conservative boundary. Common along mid-ocean ridges as transform faults.

nodes.label: Sea Floor Spreading
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process by which new oceanic crust is formed at mid-ocean ridges as plates diverge. Proposed by Harry Hess in 1960s. Magma rises from asthenosphere, solidifies, and pushes older crust laterally. Supported by symmetric magnetic striping on either side of ridges and younger rocks near ridges.

nodes.label: Subduction
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process at convergent boundaries where denser oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate into the mantle. Creates deep ocean trenches (e.g., Mariana Trench). Generates intense volcanic activity and earthquakes. Subducted material melts and recycles back as magma. Drives the rock cycle at a global scale.

nodes.label: Mid-Ocean Ridge
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Continuous underwater mountain chain formed at divergent plate boundaries. Longest mountain range on earth at about 65,000 km. Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the most prominent example, running through the center of the Atlantic Ocean. Site of active volcanism and hydrothermal vents.

nodes.label: Tethys Sea
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Ancient shallow sea that existed between Laurasia and Gondwana. Accumulated thick sedimentary deposits over millions of years. These sediments were folded and uplifted to form the Himalayan mountain chain when the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate. Closed completely about 50 million years ago.

nodes.label: Convection Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Circular movement of mantle material caused by heat from the earth's interior. Hot material rises from the core-mantle boundary, moves laterally beneath lithosphere, cools, and sinks. Proposed by Arthur Holmes as the driving mechanism for continental drift and plate tectonics.

nodes.label: Major Tectonic Plates
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Seven major lithospheric plates: Pacific (largest), North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, and Antarctic. Minor plates include Nazca, Philippine, Arabian, Caribbean, Cocos, Juan de Fuca, and Scotia. Plates include both continental and oceanic lithosphere.

nodes.label: Indian Plate
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Tectonic plate carrying the Indian subcontinent. Originally part of Gondwana, separated about 140 mya and moved northward. Collided with the Eurasian plate about 50 mya, closing the Tethys Sea and forming the Himalayas. Continues to move northward at about 5 cm/year, making the Himalayas still rising.

nodes.label: Pacific Plate
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Largest tectonic plate, almost entirely oceanic. Surrounded by subduction zones forming the Ring of Fire. Being subducted under the North American, Philippine, and Australian plates. Contains hotspot volcanism (Hawaiian Islands). Shrinking as it is consumed at convergent boundaries faster than new crust forms.

nodes.label: Ring of Fire
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific Ocean with intense seismic and volcanic activity. About 40,000 km long. Contains 75% of world's active and dormant volcanoes and about 90% of earthquakes. Caused by subduction of Pacific and other oceanic plates beneath surrounding continental plates.

nodes.label: Alfred Wegener
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: German meteorologist who proposed the Continental Drift Theory in 1912 in his book 'The Origin of Continents and Oceans'. Could not explain the mechanism of drift, which was his theory's main weakness. Proposed tidal forces and centrifugal forces as drivers, which were later disproved.

nodes.label: Ocean Floor Relief
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Major divisions of ocean floor: continental shelf (shallow, up to 200m depth, rich in resources), continental slope (steep descent to 3000m), continental rise (gentle slope), abyssal plains (flat deep floor, 3000-6000m), ocean trenches (deepest, subduction zones), and mid-ocean ridges (underwater mountain chains).

nodes.label: Continental Shelf
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Shallow submerged extension of the continent from the shoreline to the continental slope, typically up to 200m depth. Width varies greatly. Rich in marine life, fisheries, and mineral resources (oil, gas). Constitutes about 7.5% of ocean floor. EEZ extends 200 nautical miles from coast. India has a broad shelf off Gujarat.

nodes.label: Ocean Trench
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Long, narrow, deep depressions on the ocean floor formed at convergent plate boundaries where oceanic plates are subducted. Deepest features on earth's surface. Mariana Trench (11,034 m) is the deepest. Others include Tonga, Philippine, and Kuril-Kamchatka trenches. Associated with intense seismic and volcanic activity.

nodes.label: Abyssal Plain
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Flat, featureless areas of the deep ocean floor at depths of 3,000-6,000 meters. Among the flattest features on earth. Covered by fine sediments that have settled over millions of years. Cover about 40% of the ocean floor. May contain manganese nodules and other mineral resources.

nodes.label: Coral Reef
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Underwater ecosystem built by colonies of coral polyps that secrete calcium carbonate. Need warm (20-28C), clear, shallow (less than 50m depth), saline water. Three types: fringing reef (attached to shore), barrier reef (separated by lagoon, e.g., Great Barrier Reef), and atoll (circular reef around sunken island). High biodiversity.

nodes.label: Submarine Canyon
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Deep, V-shaped valleys cut into the continental shelf and slope. Formed by turbidity currents (underwater sediment flows) and possibly by river erosion when sea levels were lower during ice ages. Major examples include Monterey Canyon and Hudson Canyon. Act as sediment transport pathways to deep ocean.

nodes.label: Seamount and Guyot
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Seamounts are underwater volcanic mountains rising 1000+ meters above the ocean floor but not reaching the surface. When flat-topped (eroded by waves when at surface then submerged), called guyots/tablemounts. Often found in lines marking hotspot tracks (e.g., Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain). Biodiversity hotspots.

nodes.label: Ocean Resources
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Oceans provide multiple resources: biological (fish, seaweed), mineral (oil, gas, manganese nodules, polymetallic sulphides), energy (tidal, wave, OTEC), and transportation. Continental shelves are richest zones. Deep-sea mining is emerging. Sustainable management is critical as overfishing and pollution threaten ocean health.

nodes.label: India's Strategic Location
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India occupies a central position in the Indian Ocean region. Commands major sea routes connecting Europe, Africa with East and Southeast Asia. Suez Canal reduced the distance between India and Europe. Peninsular shape provides access to both Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Vital for trade, energy security, and geopolitics.

nodes.label: The Himalayas
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Youngest fold mountain system, formed by collision of Indian and Eurasian plates. Extends 2,400 km from Indus to Brahmaputra. Width varies from 400 km in Kashmir to 150 km in Arunachal Pradesh. Contains world's highest peaks. Three parallel ranges: Greater Himalayas, Lesser Himalayas, and Shiwaliks. Still rising.

nodes.label: Greater Himalayas (Himadri)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Northernmost and highest range with average height of 6,000m. Contains all peaks above 8,000m including Everest (8,849m), K2, Kangchenjunga. Composed of granite. Permanently snow-covered with glaciers. Nearly continuous range. Core of the Himalayan system. Nanga Parbat in the west, Namcha Barwa in the east.

nodes.label: Lesser Himalayas (Himachal)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Middle range between Greater Himalayas and Shiwaliks, 3,700-4,500m average altitude. Also called Himachal or Middle Himalayas. Contains Pir Panjal (longest range), Dhaula Dhar, and Mahabharat ranges. Famous hill stations: Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling. Kashmir Valley and Kangra Valley lie here. Width of 50 km.

nodes.label: Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Southernmost and lowest Himalayan range with 900-1100m average height. Composed of unconsolidated river deposits (alluvium, gravel). Highly susceptible to erosion. Longitudinal valleys between Shiwaliks and Lesser Himalayas called Duns (e.g., Dehradun, Patli Dun). Width of 10-50 km. Youngest Himalayan range.

nodes.label: Purvanchal (Eastern Highlands)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Hills at the eastern extension of Himalayas running south along India-Myanmar border. Include Patkai Bum, Naga Hills, Manipur Hills, Mizo Hills (Lushai Hills). Composed of strong sandstone. Covered with dense forests. Run as a series of ranges in north-south direction, in contrast to east-west Himalayas.

nodes.label: Reserved and Protected Forests
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Indian forests classified by legal status: Reserved forests (most restricted, no public activity without permission, about 53% of forest area), Protected forests (limited rights to communities, about 29%), and Unclassed forests (controlled by communities/private, about 18%). MP has the largest area under reserved forests.

nodes.label: Indian Diaspora
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Three waves: colonial indentured labour to Mauritius/Caribbean/Fiji; skilled workers to SE Asia/West Asia (1970s oil boom); professionals to USA/UK/Canada (1960s onwards). One of most powerful diasporas.

nodes.label: Surface Water
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 10,360 rivers. Mean annual flow 1,869 cubic km. Ganga/Brahmaputra/Barak have 60% though only 1/3 area. South Indian rivers largely harnessed.

nodes.label: Inland Waterways
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 14,500 km, 1% transport. NW1 Allahabad-Haldia (Ganga), NW2 Sadiya-Dhubri (Brahmaputra), NW3 Kottapuram-Kollam (Kerala).

nodes.label: Air Transport
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Started 1911. 12 international, 112 domestic airports. Air India and Indian Airlines. 52% at Mumbai/Delhi.

nodes.label: Major Ports
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 12 major. West: Kandla, Mumbai, JNPT, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi. East: Tuticorin, Chennai, Ennore, Vishakhapatnam, Paradip, Kolkata/Haldia.

nodes.label: Mumbai Port
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Natural harbour, largest port. JNPT/Nhava Sheva supplements to relieve congestion.

nodes.label: Vishakhapatnam Port
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Deepest landlocked harbour east coast. Iron ore, petroleum. AP hinterland.

nodes.label: Chennai Port
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Oldest east coast. Artificial harbour 1859. Ennore 25 km north relieves pressure.

nodes.label: Kandla Port
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Gulf of Kutch. Built to replace Karachi lost at partition. Serves western/NW India.

nodes.label: Earth's Crust
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Uppermost and thinnest layer of earth. About 35 km thick on continental masses (sial - silica and alumina) and only 5 km on ocean floors (sima - silica and magnesium).

nodes.label: Igneous Rocks
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed when molten magma cools and solidifies. Also called primary rocks. Two types: extrusive (basalt, cools rapidly on surface, fine-grained) and intrusive (granite, cools slowly inside crust, large grains).

nodes.label: Sedimentary Rocks
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed from compressed and hardened sediments transported by wind, water etc. Contain fossils of plants and animals. Example: sandstone from sand grains. Form in layers.

nodes.label: Metamorphic Rocks
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed when igneous or sedimentary rocks change under great heat and pressure. Clay becomes slate, limestone becomes marble. Greek word metamorphose meaning change of form.

nodes.label: Minerals
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Naturally occurring substances with definite chemical composition and physical properties. Used as fuels (coal, natural gas, petroleum) and in industries (iron, aluminium, gold, uranium).

nodes.label: Fossils
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Remains of dead plants and animals trapped in layers of rocks. Found in sedimentary rocks. Provide evidence of past life on earth and geological history.

nodes.label: Sial and Sima
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sial (silica + alumina) forms continental mass. Sima (silica + magnesium) forms oceanic crust. Continental crust is thicker but less dense than oceanic crust.

nodes.label: Cold Desert
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: High altitude deserts with extreme cold, thin air, low rainfall. Sparse vegetation. Examples: Ladakh, parts of Central Asia, parts of Antarctica.

nodes.label: Manali-Leh Highway
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Crosses four passes: Rohtang La, Baralacha La, Lungalacha La, Tanglang La. Opens only between July and September when snow is cleared. One of highest motorable roads in the world.

nodes.label: Types of Minerals
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Over 3000 types. Metallic (ferrous: iron, manganese, chromite; non-ferrous: gold, silver, copper, lead) and non-metallic (limestone, mica, gypsum). Mineral fuels: coal, petroleum. Identified by physical/chemical properties.

nodes.label: India's Mineral Distribution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Iron ore: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Karnataka. Bauxite: Jharkhand, Odisha, Gujarat. Mica: Jharkhand, Bihar, Rajasthan (India largest exporter). Copper: Rajasthan. Gold: Kolar, Karnataka. Salt: India leading producer.

nodes.label: Coal
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Most abundant fossil fuel. Called Buried Sunshine. Used for domestic fuel, industries, thermal power. Leading producers: China, USA, Germany, Russia. India: Raniganj, Jharia, Dhanbad, Bokaro in Jharkhand.

nodes.label: Hydel Power
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Electricity from falling water through dams turning turbines. One-fourth of world's electricity. Leading: Paraguay, Norway, Brazil, China. India: Bhakra Nangal, Gandhi Sagar, Nagarjunsagar, Damodar Valley.

nodes.label: Cotton
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Requires high temperature, light rainfall, 210 frost-free days, bright sunshine. Grows on black and alluvial soils. China, USA, India, Pakistan, Brazil, Egypt. Main raw material for textile industry.

nodes.label: Jute
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Known as Golden Fibre. Grows on alluvial soil in tropical areas. Needs high temperature, heavy rainfall, humid climate. India and Bangladesh are leading producers.

nodes.label: Jamshedpur (TISCO)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: TISCO started 1907 at Sakchi near confluence of Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers. Most conveniently located steel centre in India. Close to iron ore, coal (Jharia), manganese, Kolkata market. Water from two rivers.

nodes.label: Ahmedabad
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: On banks of Sabarmati river in Gujarat. First mill 1859. Called Manchester of India. Close to cotton growing areas. Flat terrain, humid climate, skilled labour. Recent problems from new textile centres and outdated machinery.

nodes.label: Suez Canal
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Opened in 1869, reduced distance between India and Europe. Enhanced India's central position on trade routes between East Asia and West. Important for India's maritime trade.

nodes.label: India's Major Physiographic Divisions
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Five divisions: The Himalayan Mountains, The Northern Plains, The Peninsular Plateau, The Indian Desert, The Coastal Plains and Islands. Result of tectonic plate movements over millions of years.

nodes.label: Greater Himalayas (Himadri)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Northernmost and most continuous range with average height 6000m. Contains all peaks over 8000m including Everest, K2, Kanchenjunga. Perennially snow-covered. Core of young fold mountains.

nodes.label: Lesser Himalayas (Himachal)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: South of Himadri with altitude 3700-4500m. Ranges: Pir Panjal, Dhaula Dhar, Mahabharat. Famous valleys: Kashmir, Kangra, Kullu. Hill stations: Shimla, Mussoorie.

nodes.label: Western Disturbances
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cyclonic disturbances originating over Mediterranean Sea, brought by westerly jet stream. Cause winter rainfall in NW India (Punjab, Haryana, HP). Crucial for rabi crop especially wheat.

nodes.label: Census of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Conducted every 10 years since 1872. First complete census in 1881. Provides comprehensive population data. Census 2011 was 15th census. Largest peacetime administrative exercise in the world.
